**Research question:** Where can someone find the best East Asian (Korean, Japanese, and Chinese) restaurants in New Orleans, and which neighborhood is best for finding them?

## Summary for Steps 1 to 6

**Region chosen: New Orleans Neighborhood Statistical Areas (NSA), ranking only neighborhoods with at least 5 East Asian restaurants.**

* **Why:** NSAs are official city neighborhoods with names visitors recognize, which fits a question about where to go. Census tracts were too small (median 1 restaurant per tract), and ZIP codes gave larger counts but are postal areas, not neighborhoods, and extend outside the city into Jefferson Parish. The minimum of 5 keeps 8 neighborhoods (76 of 135 restaurants) so averages do not rest on one or two restaurants.
* **Check:** The top neighborhood, St. Claude, is also inside the top ranked ZIP code (70117), so the main finding does not depend on the boundary choice.
* **Where to look:** the comparison table and three maps are in [Step 6](#step-6-compare-geographic-systems), and the reasoning is in [Decision](#decision-neighborhood-statistical-areas).

Steps 1 and 2 (import, filter to New Orleans, save RDS) are in [`R/import.R`](R/import.R). This file covers category selection (Step 3), the business to review join (Step 4), the Census place spatial join (Step 5), and the comparison of geographic systems (Step 6).

## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(knitr)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("data/boundaries", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

nola <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds")
reviews <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans.rds")

dim(nola)
dim(reviews)
```

## Step 3: Select related restaurant categories

### Split the comma separated categories

```{r}
restaurant_categories <- nola |>
  select(business_id, categories) |>
  separate_rows(categories, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(category = str_to_lower(str_squish(categories))) |>
  filter(category != "") |>
  distinct(business_id, category)

category_counts <- restaurant_categories |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE)

category_counts |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  kable(caption = "Most common categories among New Orleans restaurants")
```

### Starting point: Korean food

I started with Korean food, but only a handful of New Orleans restaurants carry the Korean category, which is below the project minimum of 10 restaurants in 7 areas.

```{r}
korean_ids <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category == "korean") |>
  distinct(business_id)

nrow(korean_ids)

restaurant_categories |>
  semi_join(korean_ids, by = "business_id") |>
  filter(!category %in% c("korean", "restaurants")) |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE) |>
  kable(caption = "Categories that appear together with Korean")
```

### Expanding to East Asian food

I expanded the theme to the East Asian food tradition that Korean food belongs to: Korean, Japanese, and Chinese, plus their sub styles (sushi bars and ramen for Japanese; dim sum, Szechuan, and Taiwanese for Chinese). Southeast Asian categories (Vietnamese, Thai) and nationality neutral labels (Asian Fusion, Noodles, Poke) are excluded so the group stays conceptually consistent.

```{r}
core_categories <- c("korean", "japanese", "chinese")
sub_categories <- c("sushi bars", "ramen", "dim sum", "szechuan", "taiwanese")
selected_categories <- c(core_categories, sub_categories)

considered <- c(selected_categories, "vietnamese", "thai", "asian fusion",
                "noodles", "poke")

category_counts |>
  filter(category %in% considered) |>
  mutate(decision = if_else(category %in% selected_categories,
                            "included", "excluded")) |>
  kable(caption = "Asian categories considered")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

category_counts |>
  filter(category %in% considered) |>
  mutate(
    decision = if_else(category %in% selected_categories, "Included", "Excluded"),
    category = fct_reorder(str_to_title(category), n)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = category, fill = decision)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Included = "#C0392B", Excluded = "grey70")) +
  labs(
    title = "Asian Restaurant Categories in New Orleans",
    x = "Number of restaurants", y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("figures/category_counts.png", width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 150)
```

### Co-occurrence among the selected categories

```{r}
selected_category_rows <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories)

selected_category_rows |>
  inner_join(selected_category_rows, by = "business_id",
             relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  filter(category.x < category.y) |>
  count(category.x, category.y, sort = TRUE, name = "restaurants") |>
  kable(caption = "Pairs of selected categories on the same restaurant")
```

### Inclusion rule

A restaurant is included if it has **at least one** of the selected categories. Each restaurant also gets one cuisine label for maps (Korean first, then Japanese, then Chinese).

```{r}
selected_ids <- selected_category_rows |>
  distinct(business_id)

selected_restaurants <- nola |>
  semi_join(selected_ids, by = "business_id") |>
  mutate(
    cat_lower = str_to_lower(categories),
    cuisine = case_when(
      str_detect(cat_lower, "korean") ~ "Korean",
      str_detect(cat_lower, "japanese|sushi bars|ramen") ~ "Japanese",
      str_detect(cat_lower, "chinese|dim sum|szechuan|taiwanese") ~ "Chinese"
    )
  ) |>
  select(-cat_lower)

nrow(selected_restaurants)

selected_restaurants |>
  count(cuisine) |>
  kable(caption = "Selected East Asian restaurants by cuisine label")
```

The group has 145 restaurants. Step 6 shows that the 135 inside the city fall in 43 different neighborhoods, so the project minimum of 10 restaurants in at least 7 geographic areas is met.

## Step 4: Join businesses to reviews

Reviews are filtered to the selected restaurants before any further analysis.

```{r}
east_asian_reviews <- reviews |>
  semi_join(selected_restaurants, by = "business_id")

review_summary <- east_asian_reviews |>
  group_by(business_id) |>
  summarise(
    n_reviews = n(),
    avg_review_stars = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

selected_restaurants <- selected_restaurants |>
  left_join(review_summary, by = "business_id")

tibble(
  restaurants = nrow(selected_restaurants),
  reviews = nrow(east_asian_reviews),
  reviewers = n_distinct(east_asian_reviews$user_id),
  restaurants_without_reviews = sum(is.na(selected_restaurants$n_reviews))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Business to review join")
```

## Step 5: Spatial join with the Census place boundary

The Yelp `city` field is a text label. Here every New Orleans restaurant is placed inside the official Census place polygon that contains its coordinates.

```{r}
la_places <- places(state = "LA", cb = TRUE, year = 2024, class = "sf") |>
  st_transform(4326)

new_orleans_boundary <- la_places |>
  filter(NAME == "New Orleans")

all_points <- nola |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

all_with_place <- all_points |>
  st_join(la_places |> select(place_name = NAME), join = st_within, left = TRUE)

all_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(city, place_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  kable(caption = "Yelp city label compared with the Census place")
```

**Mismatches.** 2,202 of the 2,259 restaurants labeled "New Orleans" by Yelp are inside the official New Orleans boundary. The other 57 have coordinates in neighboring places (Elmwood, Jefferson, Harahan, Metairie, and others), mostly in Jefferson Parish. These businesses use a New Orleans mailing address, but they are outside the city, so they are not deleted from the data; they are reported as unmatched in Step 6 and left out of the neighborhood comparison.

```{r}
all_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(place_name != "New Orleans" | is.na(place_name)) |>
  count(postal_code, sort = TRUE) |>
  kable(caption = "ZIP codes of restaurants outside the New Orleans boundary")
```

Almost all of these ZIP codes (70123, 70121, 70001, 70005 and others) belong to suburbs next to the city, which confirms that the mismatch comes from mailing addresses, not from errors in the data. The one exception is a restaurant with the Uptown New Orleans ZIP code 70115 whose coordinates fall just outside the boundary; this looks like a coordinate or boundary edge issue and is flagged for checking rather than treated as a suburban restaurant.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

selected_points <- selected_restaurants |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = "grey95", color = "grey40") +
  geom_sf(data = selected_points, aes(color = cuisine), size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Korean = "#C0392B", Japanese = "#2E86C1",
                                Chinese = "#D4AC0D")) +
  labs(
    title = "East Asian Restaurants on Yelp, New Orleans",
    subtitle = "Census place boundary of New Orleans",
    color = "Cuisine"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("figures/east_asian_points.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
```

## Step 6: Compare geographic systems

Three systems are compared:

1. **Neighborhood Statistical Areas (NSA):** City of New Orleans planning neighborhoods (data.nola.gov, dataset `exvn-jeh2`).
2. **Census tracts:** Orleans Parish tracts from TIGER/Line (2024).
3. **ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTA):** Census ZIP approximations (2020) that overlap New Orleans.

### Load the boundaries

```{r}
nsa_file <- "data/boundaries/neighborhood_statistical_areas.geojson"

if (!file.exists(nsa_file)) {
  nsa_urls <- c(
    "https://data.nola.gov/api/geospatial/exvn-jeh2?method=export&format=GeoJSON",
    "https://data.nola.gov/api/v3/views/exvn-jeh2/query.geojson?accessType=DOWNLOAD"
  )
  for (u in nsa_urls) {
    ok <- tryCatch({
      download.file(u, nsa_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
      file.size(nsa_file) > 1000
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (isTRUE(ok)) break
    if (file.exists(nsa_file)) unlink(nsa_file)
  }
}

nsa_raw <- st_read(nsa_file, quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(4326)

nsa_name_col <- grep("gnocdc_lab", names(nsa_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]

nsa <- nsa_raw |>
  transmute(area_name = str_to_title(.data[[nsa_name_col]]))

tracts_orleans <- tracts(state = "LA", county = "Orleans", cb = TRUE,
                         year = 2024, class = "sf") |>
  st_transform(4326) |>
  transmute(area_name = paste("Tract", NAME))

zcta_raw <- zctas(cb = TRUE, year = 2020, starts_with = c("700", "701"),
                  class = "sf") |>
  st_transform(4326)

zcta_col <- grep("^ZCTA5CE", names(zcta_raw), value = TRUE)[1]

zcta_nola <- zcta_raw |>
  st_filter(new_orleans_boundary, .predicate = st_intersects) |>
  transmute(area_name = .data[[zcta_col]])

boundary_systems <- list(
  "Neighborhood Statistical Area" = nsa,
  "Census tract" = tracts_orleans,
  "ZIP/ZCTA" = zcta_nola
)

map_dbl(boundary_systems, nrow)
```

### Spatial join for each system

```{r}
assign_areas <- function(points, boundaries) {
  points |>
    st_join(boundaries, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    distinct(business_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

assigned <- map(boundary_systems, \(b) assign_areas(selected_points, b))

summarise_system <- function(assigned_df, boundaries, system_name) {
  per_area <- assigned_df |>
    filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
    count(area_name)

  tibble(
    `Geographic system` = system_name,
    `Number of areas` = nrow(boundaries),
    `Areas with a restaurant` = nrow(per_area),
    `Restaurants assigned` = sum(!is.na(assigned_df$area_name)),
    `Unmatched restaurants` = sum(is.na(assigned_df$area_name)),
    `Smallest area count` = min(per_area$n),
    `Median area count` = median(per_area$n),
    `Largest area count` = max(per_area$n),
    `Areas with 5 or more` = sum(per_area$n >= 5)
  )
}

comparison_table <- imap(assigned, \(a, name)
  summarise_system(a, boundary_systems[[name]], name)) |>
  list_rbind()

comparison_table |>
  kable(caption = "Comparison of geographic systems (East Asian restaurants)")

write_csv(comparison_table, "figures/geographic_comparison.csv")
```

### Area level results

```{r}
#| results: asis
area_summary <- function(assigned_df) {
  assigned_df |>
    filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
    group_by(area_name) |>
    summarise(
      restaurants = n(),
      avg_business_stars = round(mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
      median_business_stars = median(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_reviews = sum(n_reviews, na.rm = TRUE),
      avg_review_stars = round(mean(avg_review_stars, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(restaurants))
}

area_results <- map(assigned, area_summary)

for (sys in names(area_results)) {
  cat("\n\n**Top 10 areas by restaurant count:", sys, "**\n\n")
  cat(kable(slice_head(area_results[[sys]], n = 10), format = "pipe"),
      sep = "\n")
  cat("\n")
}
```

### Maps

```{r}
map_system <- function(boundaries, area_df, system_name, file_name) {
  map_data <- boundaries |>
    left_join(area_df |> select(area_name, restaurants), by = "area_name") |>
    mutate(restaurants = replace_na(restaurants, 0))

  bbox <- st_bbox(new_orleans_boundary)

  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = map_data, aes(fill = restaurants), color = "white",
            linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_sf(data = selected_points, size = 0.9, color = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", direction = -1) +
    coord_sf(xlim = bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")]) +
    labs(
      title = paste("East Asian Restaurants by", system_name),
      subtitle = "Fill = number of restaurants in the area; dots = restaurants",
      fill = "Restaurants"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

  ggsave(file.path("figures", file_name), p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
  p
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

map_system(nsa, area_results[["Neighborhood Statistical Area"]],
           "Neighborhood Statistical Area", "map_nsa.png")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

map_system(tracts_orleans, area_results[["Census tract"]],
           "Census Tract", "map_tract.png")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

map_system(zcta_nola, area_results[["ZIP/ZCTA"]],
           "ZIP Code Tabulation Area", "map_zcta.png")
```

### Unmatched restaurants

```{r}
assigned |>
  imap(\(a, sys) a |>
         filter(is.na(area_name)) |>
         transmute(system = .env$sys, business_name, address, postal_code)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  kable(caption = "Restaurants not assigned to any area")
```

The unmatched restaurants are labeled "New Orleans" by Yelp, but their coordinates fall in Jefferson Parish (Elmwood and Jefferson), outside the city limits. This matches the Step 5 comparison of the Yelp `city` field with the Census place. They are excluded from the area comparison because they are not in New Orleans.

## Decision: Neighborhood Statistical Areas

**I chose Neighborhood Statistical Areas (NSA) as the main geographic system, and I only rank neighborhoods that contain at least 5 East Asian restaurants.**

Reasons, based on the comparison table and maps:

1. **The areas match the question.** The question is where a person should go in New Orleans to find good East Asian food. NSAs have names people actually use (French Quarter, Marigny, Central Business District), and they are official City of New Orleans planning boundaries. A ZIP code such as 70130 or a label such as "Tract 134" means little to a visitor.
2. **Census tracts are too small.** With 184 tracts, half of the tracts that contain a restaurant have only 1, and only 4 tracts have 5 or more. Averages based on one or two restaurants are not reliable.
3. **ZCTAs are the most stable but not neighborhoods.** ZCTAs give the largest areas (median 4.5 restaurants, 10 areas with 5 or more), but ZIP codes are postal routes, not neighborhoods, and the ZCTAs that touch New Orleans also extend into Jefferson Parish. Their lower unmatched count comes from including restaurants outside the city, not from better matching.
4. **NSA's weakness is small counts, which a minimum rule handles.** Many neighborhoods have only 1 or 2 East Asian restaurants, so neighborhoods with fewer than 5 restaurants are shown on the maps but not ranked. This leaves 8 neighborhoods for comparison, which still meets the project requirement of at least 7 areas.
5. **ZCTA is kept as a check.** The check below shows that the top neighborhood (St. Claude) is also in the top ZIP code, so the main finding does not depend on the boundary choice. The order of the next few neighborhoods is less certain.
6. **The minimum of 5 is a middle ground.** A minimum of 3 would rank 13 neighborhoods but many averages would rest on one or two restaurants; a minimum of 10 would leave only 2 neighborhoods, below the 7 area requirement. A minimum of 5 ranks 8 neighborhoods covering 76 of the 135 assigned restaurants (56%).

What this choice hides: neighborhoods with one excellent restaurant cannot win the area ranking, and the 10 restaurants just outside the city limits are left out.

```{r}
area_results[["Neighborhood Statistical Area"]] |>
  filter(restaurants >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_review_stars)) |>
  kable(caption = "Neighborhoods with at least 5 East Asian restaurants, ranked by average review stars")
```

### How much the minimum rule keeps

```{r}
nsa_counts <- area_results[["Neighborhood Statistical Area"]]

map(c(3, 5, 10), \(k) tibble(
  minimum_restaurants = k,
  neighborhoods_ranked = sum(nsa_counts$restaurants >= k),
  restaurants_covered = sum(nsa_counts$restaurants[nsa_counts$restaurants >= k]),
  share_of_assigned = round(restaurants_covered / sum(nsa_counts$restaurants), 2)
)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  kable(caption = "Effect of the minimum restaurant rule on NSA rankings")
```

A minimum of 3 keeps many neighborhoods whose averages depend on one or two restaurants. A minimum of 10 leaves too few neighborhoods to meet the 7 area requirement. A minimum of 5 is the middle ground.

### Check against ZIP codes

If the neighborhood result is real and not caused by where the boundaries were drawn, the highest rated neighborhoods should also sit in the higher rated ZIP codes.

```{r}
zcta_ranked <- area_results[["ZIP/ZCTA"]] |>
  filter(restaurants >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_review_stars)) |>
  mutate(zcta_rank = row_number())

zcta_ranked |>
  select(zcta_rank, area_name, restaurants, avg_review_stars) |>
  kable(caption = "ZIP codes with at least 5 East Asian restaurants, ranked by average review stars")

top_nsa <- area_results[["Neighborhood Statistical Area"]] |>
  filter(restaurants >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_review_stars)) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(area_name)

assigned[["Neighborhood Statistical Area"]] |>
  select(business_id, neighborhood = area_name) |>
  filter(neighborhood %in% top_nsa) |>
  left_join(assigned[["ZIP/ZCTA"]] |> select(business_id, zcta = area_name),
            by = "business_id") |>
  count(neighborhood, zcta) |>
  left_join(zcta_ranked |> select(zcta = area_name, zcta_rank), by = "zcta") |>
  kable(caption = "ZIP codes containing the restaurants of the top 3 neighborhoods")
```

**Result of the check.** The top neighborhood holds up under ZIP codes: all 6 St. Claude restaurants fall in ZIP 70117, which is also the highest rated ZIP code. The second and third neighborhoods are less clear. Lower Garden District falls in 70130 (rank 4 of 10), and West Riverside is split between 70115 (rank 5) and 70118 (rank 10). Larger ZIP codes mix these neighborhoods with nearby restaurants that are rated lower, so their advantage shrinks. The conclusion that St. Claude is the strongest area does not depend on the boundary choice, but the order of the next few neighborhoods does.
